intro: For two thousand years, the classics shaped who held power in China. They filled exam halls, guided emperors and spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam. They also shaped who was left out. Then, starting in the 1600s, they traveled west, into Latin, French and English.

In this unit you will follow the classics through the imperial age: the Han, the arrival of Buddhism, the exams, Zhu Xi and Neo-Confucianism, and the voices of women like Ban Zhao. Then you will follow them west with Jesuits, Enlightenment writers, James Legge and Wang Tao, and into American classrooms.

By the end, you will be able to explain how the exams worked and whom they excluded. You will be able to describe how translators shaped Western views of the classics. And you will be able to connect this history to Chinese American life, including the Exclusion Act.
bigQuestion: How did the classics shape power in East Asia, and what changed as they traveled to the West?

write.prompt: Did the imperial exams live up to Confucius's words in Analects 15.38 (Legge, 1893)? Use that passage, the exams' rules on who could sit, and Ban Zhao's Lessons for Women (paraphrased) to explain how defenders and critics have judged the system.
tips: Quote Analects 15.38 and name Legge's translation.
Give facts about who could and could not take the exams.
Attribute each view: "historians argue..." or "critics say..."
Compare views rather than judge the tradition.
Use unit words like exclusion, social mobility and jinshi.
